layers.note: A herb of subalpine and alpine meadows and open slopes; among the first to flower at snowmelt.

moisture.note: Moderately dry to moist, well-drained ground.

heat_load.note: Any aspect; abundant on open, sunny slopes.

elevation_m.note: Subalpine to alpine; about 1,300 m and up in Washington.

coldest_c.note: Across its range, coldest-month means from about −20 to 1 °C; gone below −30 °C and above 5 °C.

hard_freeze_c.note: Across its range, lows to about −42 °C borne, gone where the year's coldest night falls below about −50 °C.

warmest_c.note: Across its range, warmest-month means from about 6 to 17 °C; gone below 4 °C, where summers are too short, and above 20 °C.

degree_days_0.note: About 600 to 3,000 degree-days above 0 °C, none below 300.

degree_days_5.note: About 150 to 1,600 degree-days above 5 °C, none below 50.

moisture_index.note: A moisture index from about 0.35, gone by 0.2.

summer_rain.note: No lower limit: summer-dry Cascade summers suit it; up to about 0.55 of the year's precipitation in summer, gone by 0.75.

provenance.notes: Authored for the Mount Rainier subalpine meadow scene (Paradise, about 1,650 m) from general knowledge of the species; not yet checked against the public-domain USDA references (Silvics of North America, the Fire Effects Information System, PLANTS). Western pasqueflower grows from British Columbia and Alberta to the Sierra Nevada and Montana, in subalpine and alpine meadows (the PLANTS Database). Each climate range brackets the climate of that range, an approximate envelope read from these descriptions, not fitted to occurrence records.
